# Google Workspace Cleanup via gws CLI (Drive Dedup + Gmail Organization)

On 2026-06-25, a Google Drive cleanup and Gmail inbox organization project was run through the Google Workspace CLI (`gws`), spanning duplicate-file deduplication, OAuth/auth-stability troubleshooting, Gmail signature setup, and inbox filtering for financial/receipt emails. The session established that duplicate detection by filename/metadata alone is unreliable — content-level diffing caught a false-positive duplicate group — and traced repeated OAuth session drops to an unpublished app.

## Key Points

- **Content-level verification before duplicate deletion:** filename/size heuristics are insufficient to confirm true duplicates. A "group 180" cover-letter set of three seemingly identical files contained one file with different mid-document text; content-level diffing caught the false positive. The same scrutiny was applied to video/audio "duplicates" flagged only by filename/size.
- **No Drive files deleted without an explicit verification step:** the user manually verified a sample before approving deletion; the verified duplicate-deletion plan was only executed after user confirmation.
- **OAuth session drops traced to an unpublished app:** repeated Google Workspace auth drops were root-caused to the `gws` app being unpublished. Publishing the app and confirming granted permissions resolved the recurring auth instability.
- **Gmail organization:** the Updates inbox held 23,000+ messages; a dedicated label/filter was set up to auto-sort receipts/financial-transaction emails away from Updates. A Gmail signature was also configured.
- **Working files consolidated** to a new folder at `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\agy` for easier access; the user deferred remaining email-cleanup recommendations to Claude's discretion.

## Details

The governing principle of the session was conservatism around destructive operations, mirroring the safe-deletion discipline seen in other cleanup work. Rather than trusting the CLI's duplicate flags — which are derived from filename and metadata heuristics — the workflow inserted a mandatory content-verification step before any deletion. This caught a real false positive: a set of three cover-letter files that matched on name and size but differed in mid-document text. Had the deletion proceeded on heuristic matching alone, a genuinely distinct document would have been lost. The same content-level scrutiny was extended to video and audio files flagged as duplicates, where filename/size collisions are especially likely to be coincidental. This is a specific instance of the "verify directly, don't trust the intermediate layer" pattern: the duplicate-flag is an intermediate proxy for actual file identity, and it fails precisely when files share superficial metadata but differ in content.

The OAuth instability was a separate thread. The `gws` CLI's Google Workspace session was dropping repeatedly, interrupting the cleanup work. The root cause was that the underlying OAuth app was in an unpublished state, which imposes shorter token lifetimes and re-consent requirements; publishing the app and re-confirming the granted scopes stabilized the session. On the Gmail side, the Updates category had accumulated 23,000+ messages, obscuring actionable content; a dedicated label plus filter was created to route receipts and financial-transaction emails out of Updates automatically, and a signature was configured. The user consolidated saved working files into a new `DEV\agy` folder and deferred the remaining Gmail loose-end recommendations to Claude's judgment, confirming "all good for now" with no outstanding follow-ups.

# Scoped Commit in a Dirty Working Tree (dotclaude Repo)

When the 2026-09-19 hook fix landed in `~/.claude/settings.json`, the change was deliberately left uncommitted and handed to the user with an exact path-scoped command. The reason was the state of the surrounding working tree: `~/.claude` is the synced `erash11/dotclaude` repository, and it carried unrelated uncommitted work — a `UserPromptSubmit` skill-router hook from a separate thread, plus dirty session transcripts. Committing the repair required staging one file by path rather than the whole tree.

## Key Points

- **The prescribed command stages a single file:** `git -C ~/.claude add settings.json && git commit -m "Hooks: drop the unguarded Mac-path dcg duplicate" && git push`. The `-C` flag targets the repo without changing the working directory, and naming the path avoids sweeping in adjacent changes.
- **A dirty tree makes a blanket commit unsafe, not merely untidy.** In-flight work from another thread would be committed half-finished, and transcript churn would be pushed to a shared remote alongside a one-line config fix.
- **The commit was deferred to the user rather than performed.** The change touched a synced personal-config repo with third-party-authored pending work in it; the session recorded the exact command instead of exercising judgment about unrelated files.
- **Deferral has a cost that must be stated.** Until the commit lands, `HEAD` still carries the duplicate hook, so the other machine remains broken and a future pull can reintroduce the defect on the machine that was just repaired.
- **Transcripts are routine noise in this repo.** Session records accumulate as working-tree changes continuously, so `~/.claude` is dirty by default — path-scoped commits are the normal mode there, not an exceptional accommodation.

## Details

The general rule this instance supports is that the appropriate staging granularity is a function of the repository's baseline cleanliness. In a project repo whose tree is clean between tasks, `git add -A` is a reasonable default and an unexpected extra file is itself a useful signal. In a configuration or state repo that is dirty as a matter of course — one holding transcripts, caches, machine-local scratch, or work from concurrent threads — the same command silently bundles unrelated content into every commit, destroying the history's usefulness for bisecting or reverting a specific change. `~/.claude` is squarely in the second category, which is why the remediation was written as an explicit single-path stage.

The deferral decision is separable from the scoping decision and rests on different grounds. The repair itself was verified — JSON validated, one hook remaining in the array, all 22 top-level keys intact, backup written — so the hesitation was not about correctness of the edit. It was about authority over a synced personal repo containing another thread's unfinished hook work, where pushing would propagate a partial state to a second machine. The corresponding risk of not committing is concrete and was recorded as an action item: the Mac still pulls a `settings.json` whose `PreToolUse` array runs `dcg` twice per tool call, and the Windows fix is one `git pull` away from being reverted. This is the same "the fix is not complete until it reaches the other host" dynamic described in [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]], and it parallels the destination-and-sensitivity discipline in [[concepts/dev-github-drive-migration-policy]], where what gets committed and where is governed by explicit policy rather than by whatever happens to be in the tree.

# Connection: mRSI Measurement Noise vs. Narrative Reliance on mRSI

## The Connection

RSI-modified (mRSI) is the field-default readiness metric and has been the headline signal in multiple Baylor athlete-monitoring deliverables — the Tezino narrative project tracked Tezino's mRSI decline from 0.577 (Apr 2025) to 0.407 (Jul 2025) as its central readiness story, and the Skylar Zinnecker CMJ return-to-competition reports are built on the same VALD ForceDecks CMJ metric family. On 2026-07-22, the ForcePlate_DecisionSystem reliability analysis found that mRSI is the 2nd-noisiest of 10 CMJ metrics (8.8% typical error vs. 3.8% for Peak Power/BM) and that no CMJ metric resolves the smallest worthwhile change at weekly cadence — a direct empirical caution about leaning on mRSI as a primary signal.

## Key Insight

The tension is a matter of cadence and interpretation rather than outright contradiction. The reliability finding says mRSI is unreliable at *weekly* cadence — week-to-week swings are dominated by measurement noise. The Tezino narrative tracked mRSI at roughly *monthly* intervals (Apr/Jun/Jul) across a multi-month decline, so the trend it describes may still be real even though any single week-to-week reading would be untrustworthy. The non-obvious lesson is that a monotone multi-month mRSI decline can survive the noise that would swamp a weekly reading — but only because the change accumulated over a window long enough to exceed the typical error. This argues that mRSI is defensible as a *trend* metric over months and indefensible as a *readiness* metric week to week, and that reports leading with mRSI (Zinnecker RTC, Tezino narrative) would be more robust if a lower-noise metric such as Peak Power/BM carried the primary signal, with mRSI retained for its coordination/reactive-strength interpretability rather than its raw sensitivity.

# Connection: High Retrieval Scores Do Not Guarantee Advisor Grounding

## The Connection

The 2026-06-12 book-advisor pilot revealed a non-obvious failure mode in memsearch-backed retrieval: during acceptance testing, an off-library question about protein supplementation received 0.98 memsearch similarity scores from the Periodization library, yet the content of the retrieved entries was non-prescriptive — the entries discussed energy systems and nutrient timing tangentially, not as direct guidance on protein. Without a content-inspection layer, a retrieval score of 0.98 would have green-lit an answer that sounded grounded but was actually an extrapolation from adjacent content. The [[concepts/book-advisor-system]] correctly disclosed a grounding gap rather than answering, but this correct behavior required an explicit design decision to evaluate entry content after retrieval rather than using the score as a decision gate.

## Key Insight

Semantic similarity scores — including high ones — measure topical *adjacency*, not prescriptive *match*. A 0.98 [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] score indicates that the retrieved entry is semantically close to the query in embedding space, but says nothing about whether the entry actually provides a substantive, citable answer to the question. In domains with rich conceptual vocabulary (sports science, biomechanics, nutrition), a query about protein will retrieve entries about energy systems, metabolic pathways, or timing windows that contain the word "protein" and related concepts — scoring highly — while providing no prescriptive guidance on the protein question itself. The grounding decision cannot be delegated to the retrieval score; it requires evaluating whether the entry's *content* actually supports the response being considered.

This is a specific instance of the broader "verify directly, don't trust the intermediate layer" principle documented in [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]]: the retrieval score is an intermediate layer — a proxy for content relevance — that fails in the same way a preview server fails to represent actual browser rendering, or a repair agent's confident-looking citation fails to represent accurate authorship. The score optimizes for embedding-space proximity, not for answer quality; these come apart precisely when the domain vocabulary is rich enough that topically adjacent but prescriptively empty content scores highly. The implication for any system using memsearch for knowledge retrieval: score thresholds are appropriate pre-filters (retrieve candidates above a minimum similarity), but a content-inspection step after retrieval is architecturally necessary before committing to a grounded response.

## Evidence

- 2026-06-12 (18:08): "Off-library protein question correctly disclosed grounding gap despite 0.98 memsearch scores" — the acceptance test explicitly validated that score-based acceptance would have produced a false positive for an off-library query.
- The miss-log was designed specifically for this case: off-library disclosures are recorded even when memsearch returned high-scoring results, preserving an audit trail of cases where the score-based gate would have failed if used as the sole decision criterion.
- Structural implication documented in `CREATING-ADVISORS.md`: "Judge advisor grounding by entry *content*, not retrieval score" — this lesson was elevated to a hard-won lesson in the canonical advisor guide, not merely treated as a pilot-specific observation.

# PlayerPersonel Project State and the Missing Player-Grading System

`PlayerPersonel` is a Baylor football project under `Desktop\DEV` that, as audited on 2026-09-23, contains only a film-review starter for a single athlete (Jacorey Thomas): nine contact sheets plus a Mac-only `make_sheet.py`. It holds no written assessment, no grading criteria, no report, and no source video. The session's driving question — "does any PlayerPersonel project have a grading system?" — resolved negatively for both the local repo and its Google Drive copy, and instead located the remembered grading artifacts in an entirely different project tree.

## Key Points

- **PlayerPersonel is a starter, not a deliverable.** Nine contact sheets and a Mac-only `make_sheet.py`; moved into DEV on 9/7, committed 9/9, a single commit, clean working tree. No assessment, criteria, report, or source video.
- **The Drive copy is byte-equivalent, not a superset.** `My Laptop (2) → DEV → PlayerPersonel` matches the local repo exactly, so the Drive backup contains no grading system either — ruling out "it's in the cloud copy" without further searching.
- **The grading artifacts live elsewhere:** `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\02_SPORTS\Football\PP_Recruiting`, holding `000. BAYLOR - GRD SCALE.xlsx` and the STAQS unified grading workbooks. Despite the shared "PP" prefix, this is a different project from PlayerPersonel.
- **A near-miss candidate was excluded on content, not name.** `DEV/Football/PlayerEvals` has a post-spring workbook but contains only text notes — no numeric scoring columns or formulas — so it is not the grading system either.
- **Path staleness:** `DEV/PlayerPersonel` is the live checkout; the older handoff's `DEV/Football/PlayerPersonel` path is stale and must not be trusted.

## Details

The audit illustrates a recurring hazard in a large multi-location project estate: name similarity is a poor index into content. Three candidate locations shared naming or topical proximity — `DEV/PlayerPersonel`, `DEV/Football/PlayerEvals`, and `PP_Recruiting` — and only the third, whose name overlaps least with the user's recollection, actually held the grading scale. Resolving the question required opening each candidate and checking for the defining artifact (numeric scoring columns and formulas) rather than matching on folder name. This is the same discipline applied in [[concepts/google-workspace-cli-cleanup]], where filename/size duplicate flags were rejected in favor of content-level diffing, and in [[concepts/keystoneos-repo-intake-flow]], where OneDrive shadow repos were skipped because the drive-topology convention — not the repo name — determines which checkout is canonical.

The stale-path finding is the operational counterpart. A previous handoff document recorded `DEV/Football/PlayerPersonel` as the project location; the live checkout is `DEV/PlayerPersonel`. A handoff artifact records a path as of the moment it was written, and project moves (this one landed 9/7) silently invalidate it, so a documented path is a hint to verify rather than an address to trust. Two decisions were deferred to the user: confirming whether `PP_Recruiting`'s grading scale is in fact the system being recalled or whether a third copy remains lost in the Drive migration, and deciding what the PlayerPersonel film review should ultimately produce — a one-off scouting write-up versus a repeatable grading sheet — before any further work is done there. That second question is the more consequential one, because the two outputs imply different artifacts: a write-up terminates at Jacorey Thomas, while a repeatable sheet would need to converge with (or supersede) the existing `PP_Recruiting` scale.

# $dev-sync Repo Sweep (2026-09-23 Clean Run)

`$dev-sync` is a Codex-invoked sweep that walks every repository under `Desktop\DEV`, pushes local commits, pulls incoming ones, and reports anomalies. The 2026-09-23 run was accepted as clean: 143 repos checked and pushed, 3 pulled incoming commits, none cloned or created, and no `.from-*` conflict files generated. It is the routine counterpart to the one-time staged migration described in [[concepts/dev-github-drive-migration-policy]] — the mechanism that keeps the migrated estate synchronized afterward.

## Key Points

- **Clean-run signature:** 143 repos checked and pushed, 3 with incoming commits pulled, 0 cloned or created, 0 `.from-*` conflict files. The absence of `.from-*` files is the sweep's primary conflict indicator — their presence means a two-machine divergence needed manual reconciliation.
- **Known benign exception:** `AthleticMedicineReviews` remains an empty unversioned folder and is expected to appear as such; a recurring non-defect that would otherwise read as a miss on every run.
- **The sweep feeds work selection.** With sync clean, the session picked up `PFF_Data_Project` per its `STATUS.md`: 2026 data covers graded weeks 0–3, the Parquet exchange is complete on both machines, nothing blocking. Per-repo `STATUS.md` files act as the resumable queue.
- **Sync health is reported separately from repo health.** The same day's `daily-backup` reported `repo-behind-blocked:global-memory` and the memory compiler had 2 pending logs plus a stale compile lock reclaimed after 1531 minutes (~25.5 h) — failures in the automation layer that a clean DEV sweep does not cover.

## Details

The value of a sweep like `$dev-sync` is that it converts a 143-repo estate from something no one can hold in mind into a single pass/fail signal with a small set of named exceptions. Its output is only meaningful if the expected exceptions are documented — `AthleticMedicineReviews` as a permanently empty unversioned folder is exactly such a case, and recording it prevents a recurring benign finding from either being re-investigated each run or, worse, training the reader to ignore the anomaly section entirely. The `.from-*` conflict-file convention gives the sweep a cheap divergence detector: rather than attempting a merge across two machines, it materializes the incoming variant under a suffixed name and leaves reconciliation to a human, so "no `.from-*` files" is a positive statement that no repo diverged, not merely that no push failed.

The session's second observation is that a clean sweep in one layer says nothing about adjacent automation. The `daily-backup` job reported `repo-behind-blocked:global-memory` — the backup declining to proceed because that repo was behind its remote — and the memory compiler had accumulated 2 pending logs behind a compile lock held for 1531 minutes before being reclaimed. A lock held over a day indicates a crashed or killed holder rather than legitimate contention, and the reclamation is the recovery path; the pending-log backlog is the visible cost. This is the same class of scheduled-job drift catalogued in [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]], where periodic health-check runs surface exactly these per-task escalations, and it reinforces that "sync is clean" and "the automation stack is healthy" are independent claims requiring independent checks.

# Cross-Platform settings.json: Duplicate dcg Hook from a Mac-Absolute Path

On 2026-09-19, a hook error fired on every `Bash` and `PowerShell` tool call on the Windows machine. The root cause was that the `PreToolUse` hook array matching `Bash|PowerShell` in `~/.claude/settings.json` contained **two** `dcg` entries: an original with a hardcoded macOS absolute path (`/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg`) and a later-added guarded variant (`if [ -x "$HOME/.local/bin/dcg" ]`). The guard was added but the unguarded original was never removed, so on Windows the guarded entry exited silently while the Mac-absolute path errored on every call, and on the Mac both resolved and `dcg` ran twice per tool call. The fix was committed and pushed on 2026-09-23, four days later, after the defect had produced 49 `PreToolUse` errors in a single session.

## Key Points

- **A guard is only half a fix.** Adding a guarded variant of a hook command without deleting the unguarded original leaves both entries in the array; hook arrays execute every entry, so the broken one still fires.
- **The failure is asymmetric across machines.** On Windows the Mac-absolute path does not resolve and errors loudly on every matching tool call; on macOS both entries resolve, producing a silent double-execution rather than an error.
- **The error volume is per-tool-call, not per-session.** One 2026-09-23 session accumulated 49 `PreToolUse` errors before the fix, because the hook matches `Bash|PowerShell` and every such tool call re-triggers it.
- **`~/.claude` is a synced repo.** The directory is the `erash11/dotclaude` GitHub repo, so a Mac-absolute path committed there propagates to the Windows checkout. Machine-specific absolute paths in hook commands are a cross-platform hazard by construction.
- **The layering rule:** machine-specific hook paths belong in the guarded or `machine.md` layer, never in shared `settings.json`. Shared settings must contain only references valid on every host that pulls them.
- **Running sessions keep erroring until reload.** Sessions already open when the edit lands continue throwing the hook error; only `/hooks` or a full restart reloads settings — an action item on 2026-09-23 was to restart any long-running session.

## Details

The fix applied on 2026-09-19 was minimal: remove the unguarded entry, leaving one hook in that array. Validation confirmed the JSON parsed and all 22 top-level keys remained intact, with a backup written to `~\.claude\jobs\06c56c44\tmp\settings.json.bak-20260919`. A separate cross-platform artifact — `/Users/kristinarash/DEV` listed in `permissions.additionalDirectories` — was deliberately left alone: it is harmless on Windows (a path that simply does not exist) and required on the Mac, illustrating that not every foreign-looking absolute path in a synced settings file is a defect. The distinction is between a path that is *inert* when absent (an additional-directory grant) and one that is *executed* when absent (a hook command).

The commit was deliberately not made during the 2026-09-19 session because `~/.claude`'s working tree carried unrelated uncommitted changes — a `UserPromptSubmit` skill-router hook from a separate thread, plus dirty transcript files — making a blanket `git add .` unsafe; see [[concepts/scoped-commit-in-dirty-working-tree]]. The deferral's stated cost materialized: the defect persisted across four more days and produced 49 errors in the 2026-09-23 session before being removed, pushed, and verified (the remaining guarded hook confirmed to exit 0). The interval between a verified local fix and its commit is the interval during which both machines stay broken, which is the practical argument for closing a scoped commit in the same session rather than handing it off.

The generalized rule recorded on 2026-09-23 is a layering rule, not merely a syntax rule: machine-specific hook paths belong in the guarded or `machine.md` layer, and shared `settings.json` must be written to the lowest common denominator of every environment it will reach. This is the same shell-and-path class of hook fragility documented in [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]] (PowerShell syntax emitted into a bash-executed hook) and [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] (bare `uv` invoked from a hook whose PATH omits `~/.local/bin`). See [[connections/synced-config-must-be-host-agnostic]] for the generalization. The stale-settings symptom also recapitulates the launch-time-snapshot pattern in [[connections/windows-process-env-fixed-at-launch]] and [[concepts/claude-code-remote-control-config]]: Claude Code reads `settings.json` when a session starts, so an in-flight session's behavior reflects the file as it was at launch, not as it is on disk.

# Scoped Commit in a Dirty Working Tree (dotclaude Repo)

When the 2026-09-19 hook fix landed in `~/.claude/settings.json`, the change was deliberately left uncommitted and handed to the user with an exact path-scoped command. The reason was the state of the surrounding working tree: `~/.claude` is the synced `erash11/dotclaude` repository, and it carried unrelated uncommitted work — a `UserPromptSubmit` skill-router hook from a separate thread, plus dirty session transcripts. Committing the repair required staging one file by path rather than the whole tree. The commit was finally made and pushed on 2026-09-23.

## Key Points

- **The prescribed command stages a single file:** `git -C ~/.claude add settings.json && git commit -m "Hooks: drop the unguarded Mac-path dcg duplicate" && git push`. The `-C` flag targets the repo without changing the working directory, and naming the path avoids sweeping in adjacent changes.
- **A dirty tree makes a blanket commit unsafe, not merely untidy.** In-flight work from another thread would be committed half-finished, and transcript churn would be pushed to a shared remote alongside a one-line config fix.
- **The commit was deferred to the user rather than performed** — the change touched a synced personal-config repo with third-party-authored pending work in it.
- **Deferral has a measured cost.** The handoff was not executed until 2026-09-23, four days later; in the interim the duplicate hook stayed in `HEAD`, the Mac kept double-firing, and one Windows session logged 49 `PreToolUse` errors before the fix was pushed.
- **Transcripts are routine noise in this repo.** Session records accumulate as working-tree changes continuously, so `~/.claude` is dirty by default — path-scoped commits are the normal mode there, not an exceptional accommodation.

## Details

The general rule this instance supports is that the appropriate staging granularity is a function of the repository's baseline cleanliness. In a project repo whose tree is clean between tasks, `git add -A` is a reasonable default and an unexpected extra file is itself a useful signal. In a configuration or state repo that is dirty as a matter of course — one holding transcripts, caches, machine-local scratch, or work from concurrent threads — the same command silently bundles unrelated content into every commit, destroying the history's usefulness for bisecting or reverting a specific change. `~/.claude` is squarely in the second category, which is why the remediation was written as an explicit single-path stage.

The deferral decision is separable from the scoping decision and rests on different grounds, and the 2026-09-23 outcome allows it to be graded. The repair itself was verified on 2026-09-19 — JSON validated, one hook remaining in the array, all 22 top-level keys intact, backup written — so the hesitation was not about correctness of the edit; it was about authority over a synced personal repo containing another thread's unfinished hook work. The risk recorded at the time was concrete and materialized: for four days `HEAD` carried a `settings.json` whose `PreToolUse` array ran `dcg` twice per tool call on the Mac and errored on every matching call on Windows. The lesson is that scoping and deferring are independent choices: path-scoping is what makes a commit safe in a dirty tree, and once the scoped command is known and the edit verified, deferring it further buys nothing while leaving the defect live on every synced host. See [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]] for the defect and its eventual push.

# Connection: Documented Paths Decay — Verify the Location at Use Time

## The Connection

Both halves of the 2026-09-23 session failed on the same underlying thing: a filesystem path recorded in a durable document that was no longer valid where it was being read. In [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]], `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg` was a correct path on the machine where it was written and an invalid one on the machine that pulled it, producing 49 `PreToolUse` errors in a single session. In [[concepts/playerpersonel-project-state]], `DEV/Football/PlayerPersonel` was a correct path in the handoff document that recorded it and stale by the time it was consulted, because the project had been relocated to `DEV/PlayerPersonel` on 9/7.

## Key Insight

The two failures look unrelated — one is a cross-platform portability bug, the other a documentation-staleness bug — but they are the same defect along two different axes. A written path is a snapshot of `(location, host, time)`, and it silently decays when either the host changes (config synced to a second machine) or the time changes (the project moves). In both cases the artifact reads as authoritative: a committed `settings.json` and a project handoff document are exactly the sources one is supposed to trust, and neither carries any marker distinguishing "still true" from "was true when written."

The practical consequence is that the two axes have opposite-looking remedies that share a principle. For the host axis, the fix is to stop writing the literal path at all — use `$HOME`-relative references inside an existence guard, or push the machine-specific value down into a `machine.md`/guarded layer, so the shared document contains no host-bound reference. For the time axis, no rewriting of the path helps, because the path was never wrong — the fix is procedural: treat a documented path as a hint to check rather than an address to use, and confirm the checkout exists before acting on it. Unified: a recorded path should either be written so it cannot be host-specific, or read as evidence rather than as truth. What must never happen is the failure mode both sessions hit — silently executing against a path whose validity was assumed from the authority of the document that contained it.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-23: "49 `PreToolUse` errors this session traced to a hard-coded **Mac path in the shared `~/.claude/settings.json`**"; lesson recorded as "machine-specific hook paths belong in the guarded/`machine.md` layer, not shared settings."
- 2026-09-23: "`DEV/PlayerPersonel` is the live checkout; the older handoff's `DEV/Football/PlayerPersonel` path is **stale** and should not be trusted." The project was moved into DEV on 9/7 and committed 9/9.
- 2026-09-19: the same `settings.json` defect had already been root-caused four days earlier; the inert `/Users/kristinarash/DEV` entry in `permissions.additionalDirectories` was deliberately left in place, establishing that the hazard is an *executed* stale path, not merely a foreign-looking one.
